title: Means of a convergent sequence
problem: Let (a_n) be a real sequence converging to L. Prove directly from the definition of convergence that (a_1 + ⋯ + a_n)/n converges to L.
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around means of a convergent sequence. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: Given ε>0 choose N so |a_k−L|<ε/2 for k>N. Put C=Σ_{k=1}^N |a_k−L|. For n>N the absolute error of the mean is at most C/n+(n−N)ε/(2n). Choose n large enough that C/n<ε/2. This proves the limit, including the case C=0.
rubric: Control the tail using a single cutoff.
Show the finitely many early terms have vanishing contribution.
Obtain the required bound for every sufficiently large n.
verification_note: Statement, proof, and difficulty await independent human review.

title: Monotonicity and sparse spikes
problem: Suppose a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ⋯ ≥ 0 and Σ_{n=1}^∞ a_n converges. Prove that n a_n tends to zero. Construct a nonnegative summable sequence for which this conclusion fails when monotonicity is dropped.
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around monotonicity and sparse spikes. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: For n≥2 the block from ⌊n/2⌋+1 through n has at least n/2 terms, each at least a_n. Its sum is bounded by the summable tail after ⌊n/2⌋. Thus 0≤n a_n≤2 times that tail, which tends to zero. For the counterexample set a_{2^k}=2^(−k) for k≥1 and all other terms zero. Its sum is 1, yet 2^k a_{2^k}=1.
rubric: Use monotonicity on a block whose length is comparable to n.
Use summability to force the bound to zero.
Verify summability and failure of the limit in the proposed example.
verification_note: Statement, proof, and difficulty await independent human review.

title: Asymptotic continuity
problem: Let f:[0,∞)→ℝ be continuous and suppose lim_{x→∞} f(x) exists and is finite. Prove that f is uniformly continuous on [0,∞).
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around asymptotic continuity. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: For ε>0 take R so every value past R is within ε/3 of the limit. On [0,R+2] use uniform continuity of a continuous function on a compact interval to obtain δ≤1 for ε. For x,y within δ, if their minimum is ≤R+1 both lie in [0,R+2]. Otherwise both exceed R, so |f(x)−f(y)|<2ε/3. The same δ works everywhere.
rubric: Control pairs in the tail relative to the common finite limit.
Obtain one uniform bound on a compact interval.
Handle close pairs straddling the cutoff.
verification_note: Statement, proof, and difficulty await independent human review.

title: A moving maximum
problem: For n≥1 define f_n(x)=x/(1+n x²) on ℝ. Prove that f_n converges uniformly to zero, and determine the exact value of sup_{x∈ℝ}|f_n(x)|.
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around a moving maximum. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: For t=√n |x|, the absolute value is t/[√n(1+t²)]. From (t−1)²≥0 this is ≤1/(2√n), with equality when |x|=1/√n. The supremum therefore tends to zero, equivalent to uniform convergence.
rubric: Find a bound valid for every real x.
Prove sharpness by attaining or approaching the bound.
Use the supremum to establish uniform convergence.

title: A common intersection
problem: Let K_1 ⊇ K_2 ⊇ ⋯ be nonempty compact subsets of ℝ. Prove that their intersection is nonempty. Then construct nested, nonempty closed subsets of ℝ with empty intersection.
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around a common intersection. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: Choose x_n∈K_n. All x_n lie in compact K_1, so a subsequence converges to some x∈K_1. For fixed m its tail lies in K_m, which is closed, hence x∈K_m. This works for every m. The sets [m,∞) are closed and nested and no real number belongs to all of them.
rubric: Use compactness to produce one candidate.
Prove that the same candidate belongs to every set.

title: A derivative at one point
problem: Let f:ℝ→ℝ satisfy |f(x)−f(2)|≤3|x−2|^(3/2) whenever |x−2|<1. Prove that f is differentiable at 2 and determine f′(2).
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around a derivative at one point. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: For 0<|h|<1 the absolute difference quotient at 2 is bounded by 3|h|^(1/2). This tends to zero from both sides, hence f′(2)=0.
rubric: Form the difference quotient at the specified point.

title: Weighted concentration
problem: For every continuous f:[0,1]→ℝ prove that lim_{n→∞} (n+1)∫₀¹ x^n f(x) dx = f(1).
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around weighted concentration. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: The kernel (n+1)x^n has integral 1. Given ε>0 pick a∈(0,1) with |f(x)−f(1)|<ε/2 on [a,1]. Let M=max |f(x)−f(1)|. The absolute error on [0,a] is at most M a^(n+1), and the error on [a,1] is at most ε/2. Their sum is <ε for all sufficiently large n.
rubric: Normalize the kernel or otherwise recover the constant term.
Control f near 1 by continuity.
Show the weighted contribution away from 1 vanishes.

title: Moving observation points
problem: Let f_n:[0,1]→ℝ be functions and f:[0,1]→ℝ continuous. Suppose f_n(x_n)→f(x) whenever a sequence x_n in [0,1] converges to x. Prove that f_n→f uniformly. Give an example showing the implication can fail on ℝ even with all f_n continuous.
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around moving observation points. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: Failure of uniform convergence supplies ε>0, increasing n_j and y_j with |f_{n_j}(y_j)−f(y_j)|≥ε. Compactness gives a subsequence of y_j converging to x. At its selected indices set x_{n_j}=y_j and fill the other indices by x. The full sequence tends to x, so its selected function values tend to f(x). Continuity also gives f(y_j)→f(x), a contradiction. On ℝ take f_n(t)=max(1−|t−n|,0) and f=0. Any convergent observation sequence is bounded and eventually misses the supports, while sup f_n=1.
rubric: Select increasing indices witnessing failure and extract convergent observation points.
Apply the full-sequence assumption legitimately and use continuity of f.
Verify the observation property and failure of uniform convergence on ℝ.
verification_note: Check the subsequence-to-full-sequence step and the unbounded-domain example.

title: Matching a secant with a derivative
problem: Suppose f is differentiable on (0,1), with finite limits lim_{x↓0} f(x)/x = a and lim_{x↑1} f(x)/(x−1) = b. Prove that for each c strictly between a and b there exists t∈(0,1) with f′(t)=c. Do not assume f′ is continuous.
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around matching a secant with a derivative. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: Extend f continuously by f(0)=f(1)=0, as the ratios have finite limits. For g(x)=f(x)−cx the right derivative at 0 is a−c and the left derivative at 1 is b−c. If a<c<b, g decreases away from 0 initially in the sense g(x)<g(0) for all sufficiently small x>0, and g(x)<g(1) just left of 1. Thus neither endpoint minimizes g, and its compact-interval minimum occurs inside. If b<c<a, the same sign argument excludes both endpoints as maximizers. At the interior extremum g′=0.
rubric: Obtain valid endpoint behavior from the two ratio limits.
Force an interior extremum or justify a derivative intermediate-value argument.
Cover both orders of a and b and deduce f′(t)=c.
verification_note: Check endpoint signs, including the negative difference x−1.

title: Dense zeros and the Riemann integral
problem: Construct a bounded, nonnegative Riemann integrable f on [0,1] whose zero set is dense and whose supremum equals 1. Prove in addition that every bounded, nonnegative Riemann integrable function on [0,1] with dense zero set has integral zero.
provenance: Original wording and reference argument prepared for this study by Codex. Exercise built around dense zeros and the riemann integral. No claim of novelty for the mathematics.
reference_proof: Set f(1/2)=1 and f(x)=0 elsewhere. Its zeros are dense and its supremum is 1. For any δ∈(0,1/2), isolate 1/2 in an interval of length 2δ in a partition, for instance with endpoints 1/2±δ. The upper sum is then at most 2δ and the lower sum is 0, giving integrability. In general each nondegenerate partition interval contains a zero, so every lower Darboux sum is 0 by nonnegativity. Integrability equates the integral with the supremum of these sums.
rubric: Verify the constructed example, its supremum, and its integrability.
Use density on every nondegenerate partition interval and nonnegativity.
Use integrability to identify the value with the lower integral.
